summary: The ustaz continues the story of Halimah As-Sa'diyah by stressing two lessons: thinking well of Allah in hardship, and making du'a with certainty backed by preparation. He then discusses nursing as one of the two big elements of the Prophet's ﷺ childhood in Banu Sa'd, drawing on the Quran, a UNICEF report, the book Brain Rules for Baby and his experience of a breast-milk project. The lecture closes with a call to give nursing priority, with the support of husbands, families, society and the state, reminding us that the Quran and the sirah offer guidance on raising children.
keyPoints: Allah is with the good opinion his servant has of him, and that good opinion is tested when we are in hardship.
Du'a must be made with certainty and backed by preparation, like Abu Bakr RA who got a camel ready before the Prophet ﷺ invited him to migrate.
Halimah took the orphaned baby certain that Allah would open the door of provision, and her name is remembered as the Prophet's ﷺ wet nurse.
The Quran mentions nursing again and again, and the sharia requires financial support even when a couple separate.
According to the sources the ustaz cites, breastfeeding is linked to higher IQ, better school performance, lower obesity risk and stronger immunity.
Nursing a child is not the mother's task alone and needs the support of the husband, family, society and state.

chapters.title: Opening and the sirah for adults
chapters.summary: The ustaz opens with a quote about lactation rooms, then explains that the sirah deserves to be studied again by adults and not only by children.

chapters.title: Halimah and thinking well of Allah
chapters.summary: The ustaz recalls Halimah's stressful journey, then mentions the hadith qudsi that Allah is with his servant's good opinion of him.

chapters.title: Good opinion is tested in hardship
chapters.summary: Thinking well of Allah is tested most when hardship leaves no way out. Allah guides the heart of the one who believes.

chapters.title: Making du'a with certainty
chapters.summary: The hadith says du'a is not accepted from a heedless, uncertain heart. The ustaz warns us not to make du'a as empty words.

chapters.title: Abu Bakr's RA preparation for the Hijra
chapters.summary: Abu Bakr RA bought the best camel before the Prophet ﷺ invited him, because he was certain his du'a would be answered.

chapters.title: Certain and prepared in du'a
chapters.summary: The ustaz tells of scholars' advice to make du'a with certainty and then prepare, including the story of the istisqa prayer attended with an umbrella.

chapters.title: Du'a as the backbone of worship
chapters.summary: Du'a is our relationship and dialogue with Allah, and acts such as prayer, umrah and hajj are largely du'a.

chapters.title: Blessing in Banu Sa'd and two elements of childhood
chapters.summary: Halimah's family prospered while other villages were in drought. The ustaz names today's two focuses, nursing and play, and recommends The Thinking Muslim podcast.

chapters.title: Stunting and the breast-milk project
chapters.summary: The ustaz shares the UNICEF report on child stunting in Malaysia and its recommendation of six months of exclusive breastfeeding, and how the Susu Ibu project began.

chapters.title: Nursing in the Quran and the story of Prophet Musa AS
chapters.summary: The Quran mentions nursing again and again. The story of Musa AS and his mother shows Allah fulfilling his promise, and the sharia requires financial support during separation.

chapters.title: Brain Rules for Baby and the benefits of nursing
chapters.summary: The ustaz reads John Medina on nursing and lists four benefits: higher IQ, better school performance, lower obesity risk and stronger immunity.

chapters.title: Formula milk and misinformation
chapters.summary: The ustaz describes the project's work in low-income communities, the heavy advertising of formula and mistaken beliefs about making a child clever.

chapters.title: Exceptions and colostrum
chapters.summary: Nursing the child yourself is the first choice, and if that is not possible the child is given to a wet nurse. The ustaz stresses colostrum and that mother's milk has no equal.

chapters.title: Benefits for mother and baby
chapters.summary: Mother's milk adjusts its content to the baby's development, and studies mention benefits for the mother including a lower risk of some cancers.

chapters.title: Support from family, society and state
chapters.summary: Nursing is not the mother's job alone. Developed countries invest through long maternity leave because investing early saves costs later.

chapters.title: Closing: priorities and the Quran's guidance
chapters.summary: Do not compare yourself with others' material standards. Modernity does not guarantee a good childhood, and the Quran and the sirah give guidance from the Creator of mankind.

books.context: The ustaz reads a passage that a country wanting a smarter, healthier population would prioritise nursing, and the four benefits of nursing.
Shows that before COVID-19 one in five children in Malaysia was stunted, and recommends exclusive breastfeeding for at least six months.

lessons.title: Think well of Allah
lessons.body: Allah is with his servant's good opinion of him and remembers the one who remembers him in a better assembly.

lessons.title: Good opinion is tested in hardship
lessons.body: It is easy to think well when comfortable. The real test is when there is no way out, and there Allah guides the heart of the believer.

lessons.title: Make du'a with certainty
lessons.body: Du'a from a heedless, uncertain heart is not accepted, so avoid despair and empty words when making du'a.

lessons.title: Certainty goes with preparation
lessons.body: Abu Bakr RA made the best preparation before his du'a was answered, as a sign of real certainty.

lessons.title: Act with certainty in Allah's provision
lessons.body: Halimah did not just make du'a and sit still. She took the baby certain that Allah would open the door of provision, and her name is remembered.

lessons.title: Du'a is a dialogue, not a script
lessons.body: Du'a is our communication with Allah, so understand what is said and be sure it is heard.

lessons.title: Nursing is a child's right
lessons.body: The ustaz calls for more children to receive the right to be nursed exclusively, with the Quran's indication of up to two years.

lessons.title: Nursing is not the mother's job alone
lessons.body: A mother's success at breastfeeding depends a great deal on support from her husband, family and society.

lessons.title: Beware of advertising and misinformation
lessons.body: Advertising can make some mothers think the most expensive milk makes a child clever, leading them to overspend or dilute the milk.

lessons.title: Society and state should support nursing mothers
lessons.body: Wise countries invest early through long maternity leave because it saves health costs later.

lessons.title: A child is a trust and a top priority
lessons.body: A baby comes from Allah as a trust and a gift, so it should be a priority.

lessons.title: Do not be tied to others' material standards
lessons.body: Obsession with growth and material comparison causes stress, and needs rethinking.

glossary.meaning: A hadith the Prophet ﷺ narrated from Allah in his own words.
Having a good opinion of Allah's decree and promises, especially in hardship.
A woman who nurses another's child, like Halimah for the Prophet ﷺ.
Stunted physical growth and brain development in a child from lack of nutrition and lifestyle.
A situation where several major diseases strike at once, which the ustaz calls the triple burden.
The first yellow milk after a baby is born, rich in nutrients and antibodies.

dalil.context: The ustaz links this hadith qudsi to Halimah's good opinion of Allah's decree.
dalil.translation: Allah says: I am with my servant's opinion of me, and I am with him when he remembers me. If he remembers me in an assembly, I remember him in a higher and better assembly.

dalil.context: Whoever believes in Allah, Allah guides his heart. The ustaz mentions Surah At-Taghabun with some caution. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: Misfortunes can only happen with God’s permission––He will guide the heart of anyone who believes in Him: God knows all things––

dalil.context: The ustaz warns us not to make du'a with empty words and despair.
dalil.translation: Call upon Allah while you are certain that the du'a will be answered. Know that Allah does not accept du'a from a heedless and negligent heart.

dalil.context: The ustaz explains that prayer, umrah and hajj are largely du'a.
dalil.translation: Du'a is the backbone of worship.

dalil.context: The mother of Prophet Musa AS was told to nurse him and cast him into the river, with Allah's promise to return him. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: We inspired Moses’ mother, saying, ‘Suckle him, and then, when you fear for his safety, put him in the river: do not be afraid, and do not grieve, for We shall return him to you and make him a messenger.’

dalil.context: Musa AS refused to nurse from anyone in the palace until his sister suggested his mother, and Allah fulfilled his promise. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: We had ordained that he would refuse to feed from wet nurses. His sister approached them and said, ‘Shall I tell you about a household which could bring him up for you and take good care of him?’

dalil.context: The sharia sets specific maintenance for a divorced wife so she can nurse the child. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: House the wives you are divorcing according to your means, wherever you house yourselves, and do not harass them so as to make their lives difficult. If they are pregnant, maintain them until they are delivered of their burdens; if they suckle your infants, pay them for it. Consult together in a good way- if you make difficulties for one another, another woman may suckle the child for the father––

dalil.context: The ustaz reminds us that a baby comes from Allah and will return to him, so birth is a trust and a priority. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: those who say, when afflicted with a calamity, ‘We belong to God and to Him we shall return.’

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions the period of exclusive nursing the Quran indicates, up to two years. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: Mothers suckle their children for two whole years, if they wish to complete the term, and clothing and maintenance must be borne by the father in a fair manner. No one should be burdened with more than they can bear: no mother shall be made to suffer harm on account of her child, nor any father on account of his. The same duty is incumbent on the father’s heir. If, by mutual consent and consultation, the couple wish to wean [the child], they will not be blamed, nor will there be any blame if you wish to engage a wet nurse, provided you pay as agreed in a fair manner. Be mindful of God, knowing that He sees everything you do.

dalil.context: Allah, who created mankind, knows what is best for them, so the Quran is a guide to raising children. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: How could He who created not know His own creation, when He is the Most Subtle, the All Aware?
